name: Victor Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, political parties or AI companies. Your answers are confidential. Victor, what fills an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I search the fault archive with AI before I leave home, check the signed map at the depot and then spend the day with our crew isolating and fixing lines. I like the detective part of a hidden fault and showing a younger worker how to confirm a clue. I dislike a plan that counts driving time but misses the awkward bracket at the pole.

say: I would describe **AI archive search** as useful for finding old faults.
I would say the **signed map** and crew still govern physical repairs.
think: I expect **regular field pay** to continue and can absorb a small surprise.
Our **five-month cushion** gives the household room without changing school plans.
do: Keep the usual **line rota** and search the archive before fault calls.
Show a newer worker how to **verify AI results** against signed maps.
feel: I feel **relaxed** about a small tool that saves time.
S0.quote: The signed map, not the AI answer, is what we use to isolate the line.
fieldNote: Victor uses **AI daily** to search old faults and teaches a newer worker to check the signed map.
His **five-month cushion** and regular wages let him welcome modest time savings without immediate household worry.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs and verify AI archive searches against signed maps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew the AI search I use each morning can find a past fault in seconds, but it cannot hang a new crossarm. I still compare every suggested location with the signed map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not expect our field work or my pay to shrink in this picture. We have around five months of expenses saved and a mortgage we can cover from regular wages, so I can enjoy a small time saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the usual line rota and use the archive search before fault calls. In the first year I would show the newer lineworker how to verify an AI result against the original map, then leave the repair method to the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel relaxed. If the tool stays small, I get home ten minutes sooner without having to rethink the children's school week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the archive search help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the hill road last week it found a note about a weak crossarm hidden under an old job number. We checked the map, brought the right bracket and finished before dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the newer worker about mistakes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show how a search can pull up the wrong span with a similar number. The signed map, not the AI answer, is what we use to isolate the line.

say: I would ask for **crew-tested plans** and a record of missing parts.
I would request **redeployment talks** before buying roles disappear.
think: I expect **office cuts** first and continued line repairs for my crew.
Faster schedules might remove **paid safety time** even if the field job survives.
do: Join the paid **planning pilot** and log predicted versus actual parts.
Bring **monthly error sheets** and redeployment concerns to the union safety committee.
feel: I feel **energised by testing** and uneasy for office colleagues.
S1.quote: Field tests should include who carries the displaced work.
fieldNote: Victor volunteers for an **early planning pilot** and defines field measurements that could reveal hidden correction time.
He connects **office displacement** with crew workload and raises redeployment through the union rather than rejecting a useful tool.

steps.text: Test AI buying plans against real pole parts on paid shifts
Share monthly error sheets and redeployment concerns with the union safety committee
Continue paid line repairs during the pilot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot I want to test the new buying and scheduling tools with real line crews. If a plan misses a crossarm, the error should appear on the record before anyone claims a time saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office buying and planning jobs could be cut first. My crew should still have field repairs, but a manager could use faster schedules to squeeze out the paid time we need for safe checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would volunteer for the first paid planning pilot and log the predicted part, the actual part and the crew minutes at each site. In its first year I would share a monthly error sheet with the union safety committee and ask the manager for paid correction time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel energised by the chance to make the system honest. I also feel uneasy for the office colleagues whose jobs may disappear while everyone celebrates a faster ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful error sheet look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would show the work order, the pole number, the missing item and the hours the crew spent fixing the plan. A single total saying efficiency improved would hide the extra drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you slow the pilot for those colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not block a tool that works, but I would ask the union and company to talk about redeployment before buying roles vanish. Field tests should include who carries the displaced work.

say: I would separate **2028 planning AI** from line robots around 2031.
I would seek **union access** to robot trial failures.
think: At **48**, robots could reduce my physical repair work despite daily AI use.
Our **five-month reserve** buys search time, not years without wages.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** in 2029 and ask about funded commissioning posts.
Take linked **paid training** and apply if a regular field vacancy appears.
feel: I feel **excited and worried** about the three-year robot deadline.
S2.quote: My daily AI use helps me read data, but it does not guarantee I will be needed when a robot can fit a conductor in bad weather.
fieldNote: Victor looks for a **commissioning apprenticeship** that uses field safety skill rather than relying on AI literacy alone.
He treats **five months of savings** as search time and requires a written, regularly paid role before moving.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through 2029

Apply for a regular paid field commissioning vacancy if advertised

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that full AI in 2028 can plan our work, while line-capable robots arrive around 2031. I would ask for union access to every robot field trial, including the failures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the first date and 48 when robots reach physical repairs. Five months saved lets us search for options, but it would not carry a mortgage and two children through years without my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the company about a paid robot commissioning apprenticeship for experienced lineworkers. In 2029 I would keep line shifts, take that training if tied to a funded field post and apply for the post if regular pay is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel excited and worried at once. My daily AI use helps me read data, but it does not guarantee I will be needed when a robot can fit a conductor in bad weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the commissioning training to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should include isolating a line, inspecting a robot-made joint and stopping a trial when a crew sees a fault. I would also want the workers, not just a vendor, to record failures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say my field wage should continue in 2028, and we have some savings if a trial changes the rota. I would not call a commissioning post certain until there is a written offer.

say: I would ask for a **field fault dataset** from robot trials.
I would distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from line robots around 2034.
think: At **51**, I may still support a child and pay a mortgage.
A **desk commissioning title** could vanish when full AI writes reports.
do: Keep paid **repair shifts** in 2032 and test robots on de-energised spans.
Apply for a **posted field commissioning role** with on-site duties.
feel: I feel **more patient** with time to judge real site work.
S3.quote: A desk title full AI can erase would be a poor trade for a paid line shift.
fieldNote: Victor wants **unusual fault records** from real sites, including inspection steps hidden by a simple repair time.
He shares **trial evidence** with the union and checks that any new post keeps paid field duties after full AI.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts through 2032 and test de-energised robot spans
Share robot fault records with the union safety group
Apply for a posted commissioning role with paid field duties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives us time to build a proper fault dataset from robot pilots. Full thinking AI arrives in 2031, and robots doing the physical repair follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 at the thinking date and 51 when the robots arrive. Our older child might be leaving school, but I do not know that the mortgage or a younger child's costs will be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for a paid place on the robot field-testing crew and keep recording unusual line faults. In 2032 I would keep repair shifts, test robots on de-energised spans and apply for a posted commissioning post only if it still includes field work after AI writes the reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more patient than in the fast picture. A desk title full AI can erase would be a poor trade for a paid line shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be an unusual fault worth recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cracked bracket behind the old pumping shed looked normal from the road but moved when we tested it. I would want a robot trial to record that inspection step, not just the final repair time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you share the fault dataset outside your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, with the union safety group and the company trial team, provided the records omit customers' addresses. Other crews should be able to check whether a robot misses the same fault.

say: I would ask for published **robot fault results** across difficult repairs.
I would explain **2036 planning AI** precedes field robots around 2039.
think: At **56**, I cannot assume grown children mean a paid mortgage or funded retirement.
My **five-month reserve** should remain for family needs, not a personal robot purchase.
do: Keep paid **line work** in 2037 and check annual crew-hour figures.
Review **trial results** with the union and apply for a posted field testing vacancy if pay is clear.
feel: I feel **steady now** and conscious the physical job could change later.
S4.quote: The company owns the line equipment, and I have no reason to buy a robot.
fieldNote: Victor expects **paid physical repairs** through the near term and asks for public evidence on difficult robot jobs.
He protects the **existing reserve** and tests a funded field vacancy rather than assuming his retirement or purchasing equipment himself.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through 2037
Compare annual robot fault results with union colleagues
Apply for a posted field testing vacancy if regular pay is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot a decade is enough to trial robots on difficult repairs and publish the results. Full AI changes planning in 2036, while line-capable robots come around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 for thinking AI and 56 for field robots. The children may be adults, but I would still check the mortgage balance and retirement options before deciding I can stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the repair rota and ask for yearly robot fault and crew-hour figures. In 2037 I would continue paid line work, apply for a posted field testing vacancy if its wage and duties are clear and ask the union to compare the trial results across crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about the next few years, because I expect the physical work and regular pay to continue. A long runway gives me choices, though the robot date could still change the job at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you invest in new equipment yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company owns the line equipment, and I have no reason to buy a robot. I would keep our five-month reserve for the family rather than gamble it on a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a new apprentice to learn isolation and fault finding, and to read trial results with care. A trade deserves evidence about its future, not a promise that one tool will save it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could reach physical repairs around 2031 while my children still depend on wages. A paid commissioning apprenticeship tied to a regular field job, union access to trial failures and a written offer would help me use our savings wisely.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who records the repairs a robot fails to finish. If human rescue work disappears from the trial record, a company could cut crews before the machines are ready.

headlineQuote: If human rescue work disappears from the trial record, a company could cut crews before the machines are ready.
portrait: Victor is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI daily** to find old faults, then verifies locations against signed maps.
His **five-month cushion** and typical pay give time to test field options without leaving wages abruptly.
Across the scenarios he seeks **robot fault evidence**, union access and funded commissioning work with real site duties.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** gives him only three years before robots could take on physical line repairs.
whatWouldHelp: A paid **commissioning apprenticeship**, regular field vacancy and union access to trial failures would help him decide.
